The wildfire moved fast. Faster than anyone predicted. By the time evacuation orders went out, the flames had already jumped the highway. Twelve hundred homes burned in seventy-two hours. The fire department was outmatched from the start -- understaffed, underfunded, and facing winds that topped sixty miles per hour. Climate scientists had warned about this exact scenario for years. Longer droughts. Drier brush. Hotter temperatures. The conditions were a textbook setup for catastrophe. Insurance companies are now pulling out of the region entirely. Homeowners who rebuilt after the last fire cannot get coverage for the next one. The governor promised aid. Federal funds trickled in slowly. Displaced families lived in hotel rooms and relatives' basements for months. Fire season used to be a season. Now it is a permanent condition. The old playbook is useless. We need a new one -- and we need it yesterday.
